greek: Ὁ δὲ ὄφις ἦν φρονιμώτατος πάντων τῶν θηρίων τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ὧν ἐποίησεν κύριος ὁ θεός· καὶ εἶπεν ὁ ὄφις τῇ γυναικί Τί ὅτι εἶπεν ὁ θεός Οὐ μὴ φάγητε ἀπὸ παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ;
hint: The adjective for the serpent is the one Jesus tells his disciples to be.

notes.text: Middle Liddell gives one sense, *a serpent, snake*. The noun carries no judgement of its own; what the serpent is, the verse says with an adjective.

Superlative of φρόνιμος, whose first sense is *in one's right mind, in one's senses*; *staid, discreet* is its second and *wise, sensible, prudent* its third. It is not a word for cunning, and it is the adjective of Matthew 10:16: γίνεσθε οὖν φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις. [[flag]] Hebrew *ʿārûm*, *shrewd, crafty*, puns on *ʿărûmmîm*, *naked*, in 2:25. Greek γυμνοί and φρόνιμος share nothing, and the pun is gone.

notes.lemma: τῶν θηρίων τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
notes.text: *The wild animals upon the earth.* [[flag]] The Hebrew has *ḥayyat haśśādeh*, *the living things of the field*. The Greek widens the field to the earth, and does so again at 3:14.
The chapter's first κύριος: the title the Greek sets in place of the Hebrew divine name, as at 2:8.

τί in the accusative with ὅτι, *why is it that* — the construction of Luke 2:49, Τί ὅτι ἐζητεῖτέ με. [[flag]] The Hebrew *ʾap kî-ʾāmar ʾĕlōhîm* is an exclamation as much as a question, *Indeed, has God said…*; the Greek asks for God's reason.

οὐ μή with the aorist subjunctive, the strongest denial Greek has: *by no means may you eat*. At 2:16 every tree but one was given; the serpent's version forbids them all, and the construction makes the overstatement emphatic.
Capitalised because each opens direct speech — the serpent's question, and the words it puts in God's mouth, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take them for a proper name.

greek: καὶ εἶπεν ἡ γυνὴ τῷ ὄφει Ἀπὸ καρποῦ ξύλου τοῦ παραδείσου φαγόμεθα,
hint: The woman answers the serpent's 'no tree' with the permission as it was given.

notes.text: Future of ἐσθίω, *we will eat*, as φάγῃ was future at 2:16. The sentence does not end here: Rahlfs prints a comma, and the prohibition follows in 3:3.
καρπός is *fruit* first, then *produce, returns, profits*, then *result*. The tree has not been said to bear fruit before this verse; 2:16 gave *every tree*.
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

hint: The woman adds a prohibition the command in 2:17 does not contain.

notes.text: *Nor may you touch it.* The command as 2:16–17 gives it, in Greek and in Hebrew alike, says nothing of touching. The woman's report adds it.

Middle of ἅπτω. The entry's first sense, *to fasten, bind fast*, is the active; its second is marked *Mid.* and takes the genitive, as here — *to fasten oneself to, cling to, hang on by, lay hold of, grasp, touch*. The headword takes that sense, the form's own.
Masculine. The pronoun takes up the fronted ἀπὸ καρποῦ, repeating its preposition, not the neuter ξύλον beside it: it is the fruit that may not be eaten or touched.

notes.lemma: ὅ ἐστιν ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ παραδείσου
notes.text: At 2:9 it was the tree of life that stood ἐν μέσῳ; the woman places the forbidden tree there. Revelation 2:7 describes the tree of life with nearly the same clause: ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ τοῦ θεοῦ.

An adverb of place in the lexicon's first sense, *there, where*, and a conjunction in its second, *that, in order that*. Used as a conjunction, it takes the first conjunction sense, as a word used as a noun takes the first noun sense.
Capitalised because it opens direct speech — the command as the woman repeats it, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

greek: ᾔδει γὰρ ὁ θεὸς ὅτι ἐν ᾗ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε ἀπʼ αὐτοῦ, διανοιχθήσονται ὑμῶν οἱ ὀφθαλμοί, καὶ ἔσεσθε ὡς θεοὶ γινώσκοντες καλὸν καὶ πονηρόν.
hint: The Hebrew can be read 'like God' or 'like gods'; the Greek has to choose.

notes.text: Pluperfect of οἶδα, whose perfect is a present, *I know*; its pluperfect is a past, *knew*. [[flag]] The Hebrew *yōdēaʿ* is a participle, *God knows*. The Greek puts the knowing in the past.

notes.lemma: ἐν ᾗ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε ἀπʼ αὐτοῦ
notes.text: God's words from 2:17, ᾗ δʼ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε ἀπʼ αὐτοῦ, taken up with ἐν added — and given another ending.
Plural: *as gods*. [[flag]] Hebrew *kēʾlōhîm* can be read *like God* or *like gods*, since *ʾĕlōhîm* is plural in form either way. The Greek must decide, and decides for the plural.
One Middle Liddell entry holds two words: ὥς, accented, the demonstrative *so, thus*, and ὡς, the relative *as*. Rahlfs prints the relative, and its glosses are the chain.
γινώσκω, not οἶδα: the verb of the tree's name at 2:17, knowledge come by. Present participle — knowing as a lasting condition.
Used as a noun, and so takes καλός's first noun sense, *beauty*, as at 2:9; πονηρόν keeps the adjective's senses, the entry giving its neuter none.

hint: The Hebrew says he ate; the Greek says they ate.

notes.text: Three things seen: *beautiful* for eating, *acceptable* to the eyes to look at, and *produced at the right season* to observe. κατανοέω is *to observe well, to understand* — to take something in with the mind. [[flag]] The Hebrew has *a delight to the eyes* and *desirable to make one wise*, *lĕhaśkîl*. The Greek keeps the looking and loses the wanting: nothing in the sentence desires wisdom.
Third plural, *they ate*. [[flag]] The Hebrew *wayyōʾkal* is singular, *and he ate*. The Greek has the man and the woman eat together.
καί here is *also*: she gave also to her man. ἀνήρ, the male, as at 2:23 — not ἄνθρωπος.
μετά with the genitive opens at *in the midst of, among*; *along with* is its second sense and *with* its third. The Hebrew has the same, *ʿimmāh*, *with her*.

hint: The eyes are opened, as the serpent promised, and what they see is that they are naked.

notes.text: The serpent's verb from 3:5, διανοιχθήσονται, now in the aorist: the promise is kept in the words it was made in. διανοίγω is *to open*; its second sense, *to open and explain*, is the New Testament's — Luke 24:32, ὡς διήνοιγεν ἡμῖν τὰς γραφάς.
γινώσκω, the verb of the tree at 2:17 and of the promise at 3:5. What they come to know is that they are naked.
The word of 2:25, where it stood beside *not ashamed*, and the same imperfect, ἦσαν. γυμνός runs on to *unarmed, uncovered*.
*A girdle round the loins, apron* — a band, not a garment. Hebrew *ḥăgōrōt*, belts, is the same.

hint: The Hebrew has the wind of the day; the Greek has the evening.

notes.text: Accusative of time, *at evening*. Middle Liddell files δειλινός as a contraction of δειελινός and gives that entry one sense, *at evening*, so there is no range to open and it stands as plain text. [[flag]] The Hebrew is *lĕrûaḥ hayyôm*, *at the wind of the day* — *rûaḥ*, the word behind πνεῦμα at 1:2. The Greek gives the hour and drops the wind.

φωνή's first sense is *a sound, tone*; *the voice* follows it. The participle is genitive masculine, so it goes with κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ, not with φωνήν: the sound of the lord God, walking. Hebrew *qôl* is likewise both sound and voice.
Aorist passive of κρύπτω, *were hidden*. The entry gives the passive its own gloss, *to hide oneself, lie hidden*, and the chain carries both.
*From face* — πρόσωπον again, and here the Greek keeps the Hebrew's *face*, *mippĕnê*, as it did at 2:6.
First occurrence in this chapter, so glossed again.

notes.text: Masculine, where σπέρμα before it is neuter; a pronoun agreeing with it would be αὐτό. The Hebrew *hûʾ* is masculine and agrees with *zeraʿ*, which is masculine in Hebrew. σπέρμα's first sense is *that which is sown* — the seed of plants — then *offspring, issue*, then *race, descent*.

notes.text: τρίβολος is first *a caltrop*, a three-spiked iron thrown down to lame an enemy's horses; *a prickly plant, a burr, thistle* is its second sense, marked New Testament. Hebrews 6:8 has the pair from this verse: ἐκφέρουσα δὲ ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους.
ἀνατέλλω, the verb of 2:5, where nothing had yet risen up from the ground.
χόρτος and ἀγρός as at 2:5, where there was not yet any χόρτος ἀγροῦ. Now the man is to eat it.

greek: ἐν ἱδρῶτι τοῦ προσώπου σου φάγῃ τὸν ἄρτον σου ἕως τοῦ ἀποστρέψαι σε εἰς τὴν γῆν, ἐξ ἧς ἐλήμφθης· ὅτι γῆ εἶ καὶ εἰς γῆν ἀπελεύσῃ. —
hint: Dust in the Hebrew, earth in the Greek, and the verb for returning comes too early.

notes.lemma: γῆ εἶ καὶ εἰς γῆν ἀπελεύσῃ
notes.text: [[flag]] The Hebrew is *ʿāpār ʾattâ wĕʾel-ʿāpār tāšûb*, *dust you are and to dust you will return*. The Greek has γῆ, *earth*, both times — not the χοῦς of 2:7 — and for *return* it has ἀπέρχομαι, *to go away, depart*. The verb of returning, ἀποστρέφω, stands earlier in the verse, for the Hebrew's first *šûb*.

ἕως with the articular infinitive, a construction Middle Liddell cites in the entry itself, ἕως τοῦ ἀποτῖσαι. ἀποστρέφω's first sense is transitive, *to turn*; here σε is its subject, and the use is the entry's intransitive, *to turn back*.
*Out of which you were taken* — the verb of the rib at 2:22–23, now of the man and the earth.
Rahlfs's paragraph dash, as after 2:20. It stands in the Greek line and not in the reading.

greek: καὶ ἐκάλεσεν Αδαμ τὸ ὄνομα τῆς γυναικὸς αὐτοῦ Ζωή, ὅτι αὕτη μήτηρ πάντων τῶν ζώντων.
hint: The Greek translates her name, and so keeps the pun the Hebrew makes on it.

notes.text: Hebrew *Ḥawwâ*, which the verse itself ties to *ḥay*, *living*. The Greek does not transliterate the name but translates it — Ζωή, *life* — and Rahlfs capitalises it as a name.
Translating the name keeps the verse's reason intact: Ζωή, because she is mother of all τῶν ζώντων. [[flag]] At 4:1 the Greek transliterates the same name, Ευαν, and the play is not made again.
No verb: *this one, mother of all the living*. The Hebrew has *hāyĕtâ*, *she was*.

greek: Καὶ ἐποίησεν κύριος ὁ θεὸς τῷ Αδαμ καὶ τῇ γυναικὶ αὐτοῦ χιτῶνας δερματίνους καὶ ἐνέδυσεν αὐτούς. —
hint: Garments of skin, and the verb is one of clothing someone else.

notes.text: χιτών is *the garment worn next the skin, a frock* — the tunic, with a mantle over it — and δερμάτινος is *of skin, leathern*. The περιζώματα of 3:7 were girdles; these are garments.
ἐνδύω's first sense, *to go into, put on*, is dressing oneself; the entry marks the aorist ἐνέδυσα causal, *to clothe* another, and that is this form. They are clothed; they do not dress.
Rahlfs's paragraph dash again, in the Greek line and not in the reading.

greek: καὶ εἶπεν ὁ θεός Ἰδοὺ Αδαμ γέγονεν ὡς εἷς ἐξ ἡμῶν τοῦ γινώσκειν καλὸν καὶ πονηρόν, καὶ νῦν μήποτε ἐκτείνῃ τὴν χεῖρα καὶ λάβῃ τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς καὶ φάγῃ καὶ ζήσεται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.
hint: Three verbs of what may happen, and a fourth of what will.

notes.text: Rahlfs prints ὁ θεός alone, with Codex Coislinianus (M). [[flag]] Codex Alexandrinus reads κύριος ὁ θεός, and Origen's recension carries κύριος under the asterisk — his sign for words in the Hebrew that the Greek lacked. The Hebrew has *YHWH ʾĕlōhîm*.
[[flag]] Hebrew *hāʾādām*, with the article: *the man*. The Greek reads the name.
Perfect of γίνομαι: not *became* but *has come to be*, and stands so.
First person plural in God's mouth, as ποιήσωμεν at 2:18. The Greek renders it exactly and adds nothing to explain it.

Three subjunctives under μήποτε — *lest he stretch out, take, eat* — and then a future indicative, ζήσεται, *and he will live*: the last verb states an outcome, not a fear. Neither the Greek nor the Hebrew finishes the sentence; what God does follows in 3:23.

αἰών is first *a period of existence, one's life-time*, then *an age*, then *a long space of time*; the lexicon records εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας as *for ever*. The idiom is noted here and the reading prints the lexicon's range.
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.
Used as a noun, and so takes καλός's first noun sense, *beauty*, as at 2:9; πονηρόν keeps the adjective's senses, the entry giving its neuter none.

greek: καὶ ἐξαπέστειλεν αὐτὸν κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἐκ τοῦ παραδείσου τῆς τρυφῆς ἐργάζεσθαι τὴν γῆν, ἐξ ἧς ἐλήμφθη.
hint: This time the Greek translates Eden instead of transliterating it.

notes.text: *The park of softness, of luxury.* [[flag]] The Hebrew is *gan-ʿēden*, *the garden of Eden*. At 2:8 and 2:10 the Greek transliterated the name, Εδεμ; here it translates it with τρυφή — *softness, delicacy, luxury* — the sense *ʿēden* has as a common noun.
ἐξαποστέλλω, a double compound, ἐκ and ἀπό with στέλλω: *to send quite away*.
The task of 2:5, where there was no man to work the earth, and of 2:15, where he was set in the park to work it. The same verb, now outside.

greek: καὶ ἐξέβαλεν τὸν Αδαμ καὶ κατῴκισεν αὐτὸν ἀπέναντι τοῦ παραδείσου τῆς τρυφῆς καὶ ἔταξεν τὰ χερουβιμ καὶ τὴν φλογίνην ῥομφαίαν τὴν στρεφομένην φυλάσσειν τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς.
hint: The verb that set the man to guard the garden in 2:15 now guards it against him.

notes.text: [[flag]] The Hebrew has *wayyaškēn miqqedem lĕgan-ʿēden ʾet-hakkĕrubîm*, *and he stationed east of the garden of Eden the cherubim*. The Greek makes the man the object — he *settled him opposite* the park — and gives the cherubim a verb of their own, ἔταξεν.
κατοικίζω, *to remove to a place, and settle or establish there as colonists*: the verb of founding a colony.

Transliterated, and neuter here, τά. Rahlfs prints the Hebrew plural ending in -ιμ; Codex Alexandrinus has -ιν, as Hebrews 9:5 does, Χερουβὶν δόξης. τάσσω is *to arrange, put in order*, first of troops drawn up for battle.

Middle Liddell has no φλόγινος; LSJ gives *flaming, fiery* and cites this verse. ῥομφαία is *a large sword, scymitar*, a Thracian blade — the word of Luke 2:35 and of the sword from the mouth in Revelation 1:16. The participle is middle or passive, and the entry's passive and middle open *to turn oneself, to turn round*.

φυλάσσω, *to keep watch and ward*, the verb of 2:15, where the man was set in the park to guard it. The lexicon prints two entries under ὁδός; the first is the Attic word for *a threshold*, and the way is the second.
